messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Financial Analyst
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 65

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Smell): Related smells, Darkness: Dark spaces, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over, Auditory Recall: When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event., Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Thought Avoidance: If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it, Constant Vigilance: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next

Vignette:
Keanu, a 63-year-old financial analyst, presented as a man holding himself with rigid control, his posture betraying a tension that his quiet voice tried to conceal. The event that had upended his meticulously ordered life occurred seven months prior, on a rainy Tuesday evening. Driving home from the office, a car on the opposite side of the highway hydroplaned, crossing the median and hitting him head-on. The world dissolved into a screech of tires and a sickening crunch of metal. He remembers the sudden, violent deployment of the airbag, the acrid smell of its chemical propellant mixing with the sharp scent of leaking gasoline. Then, there was only absolute blackness and the sound of his own ragged breathing, trapped in the compressed space of the driver's seat. For what felt like an eternity, he listened to the distant sounds of approaching sirens, certain that another car would plow into his wreckage at any moment.

In the weeks that followed his physical recovery, a different kind of injury made itself known. Keanu found that the world was no longer a safe or predictable place. He had come to believe that he had to be on guard all the time, that catastrophe could strike without warning, just as it had on the highway. This belief manifested in a constant, exhausting state of alert. At his downtown office, he could no longer use the underground parking garage. The dim lighting and the lingering smell of exhaust were too similar to the crash site. The moment he would enter the darkness, his body would react before his mind could catch up; his heart would hammer against his ribs, sweat would bead on his forehead, and he would feel an overwhelming urge to flee back into the daylight. This forced him to park several blocks away, adding a stressful walk to a commute he already dreaded.

The trauma was not a memory but a recurring, present-tense event. A car backfiring on the street below his office window could instantly bring the full memory back without warning. Suddenly, he would not be at his desk but back in the crushed metal, the phantom sound of twisting steel echoing in his ears as if it were happening right now. He was certain that if he allowed himself to truly think about the event, to let the memory play out, he would not be able to handle it. This fear led him to meticulously curate his life. He stopped driving entirely, relying on his wife, Malia, or ride-sharing services, a change that strained their sense of partnership and his own independence.

His vigilance permeated every aspect of his life. When entering a restaurant with Malia, he would not sit until he had scanned for all the exits, a habit she initially found peculiar and now saw as a painful symptom. At home, sleep offered little respite. He would wake multiple times during the night, heart pounding, listening for any unusual sound, his mind racing to check whether he and Malia were safe. He understood on some level that this was not rational, but he felt compelled, believing he had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. The feeling of being unsafe was relentless. It was the accumulation of these moments—the arguments over his refusal to drive, the palpable worry in Malia’s eyes, and a particularly severe panic attack in a darkened conference room at work—that finally convinced him to seek help. He came to therapy not with a clear hope for recovery, but with a desperate fear that if something did not change, the vigilant guard he had become would completely erase the man he once was.
